Overview

Burundi at a Glance

Burundi is a landlocked East African state with a largely agrarian economy, a capital function split between Gitega and the commercial centre of Bujumbura, and a legal system in the French and Belgian civil law tradition. For investigators, the defining features are thin public data and limited online access. Company extracts are issued through the Registre du Commerce et du Crédit Mobilier at the Commercial Court in Bujumbura rather than through a public search portal, and there is no beneficial ownership register. A first comprehensive personal data protection law was promulgated in March 2026, although the supervisory agency it creates is not yet operational.

Organisations commission work touching Burundi mainly because of commodity, aid and cross-border trade exposure. Coffee accounts for most foreign exchange earnings, and gold, tin, tantalum and tungsten raise sourcing and origin questions, particularly in a region where conflict-minerals rules apply. Published anti-corruption research describes risks in customs, foreign exchange allocation, land titling, public procurement and security-sector contracting. Development organisations, buyers, lenders and investors therefore ask for counterparty background checks, verification of licences and ownership, and integrity reviews of local partners before committing funds, goods or reputation to a relationship in the country.

Legal Environment

How the law shapes investigative work involving Burundi

Legal system

Burundi has a civil law system derived from the Belgian and French codified tradition, with customary practice still relevant in land and family matters. Legislation is drafted and published in French, and laws are cited by number and date, for example Law No. 1/03 of 10 March 2026. Commercial matters are heard by the Commercial Court (Tribunal de Commerce) in Bujumbura, which also maintains the commercial register, with appeals through the courts of appeal to the Supreme Court. Companies are governed by the Code of Private and Public Companies. We have not verified the current activity of any domestic arbitration centre, so dispute resolution clauses are reviewed with local counsel.

Data protection

Law No. 1/03 of 10 March 2026 on the Protection of Personal Data, alongside Law No. 1/10 of 16 March 2022 on the Prevention and Repression of Cybercriminality · Regulator: Personal Data Protection Agency (created by Article 42 of the 2026 law; reported as not yet operational as of April 2026)

Until 2026 Burundi relied on sectoral confidentiality rules in banking, health, labour and telecommunications law. The 2026 law now requires a lawful basis for processing, including consent, contract, legal obligation or a legitimate interest that does not override the individual's rights, and restricts sensitive categories such as ethnic origin, political opinion, health and biometrics. Transfers abroad require an adequate level of protection, approved safeguards or explicit consent, and no adequacy list had been published as of March 2026. Penalties are primarily criminal. For investigative work, this means personal data collected in Burundi is minimised, handled on a documented lawful basis and transferred out only on a reviewed footing.

Private investigators

We have not identified a dedicated statute or licensing authority for private investigators or detective agencies in Burundi, and we treat the position as unconfirmed rather than permissive. Security, intelligence and policing functions are closely held by the state, and field enquiries by foreign-linked parties can attract scrutiny. Interception of communications, unauthorised access to systems and misuse of personal data are offences under the 2022 cybercrime law and the 2026 data protection law. Any local enquiry is therefore scoped with Burundian counsel, limited to lawful methods such as registry and court document retrieval and consented interviews, and carried out only by appropriately qualified local professionals.

Corporate & public records

Company records are held in the Registre du Commerce et du Crédit Mobilier (RCCM), administered through the Commercial Court in Bujumbura under the supervision of the Ministry of Justice. There is no documented public online search; extracts are generally obtained in person or through a local agent, and fees and turnaround are not published. Business creation has been digitised through the easybusiness.bi platform led by the Burundi Development Agency, but this does not provide public ownership data. No beneficial ownership register has been identified. Senior officials must declare assets under Article 146 of the Constitution, but the declarations are not public. Land records are reported to be a recurring area of irregularity.

Anti-corruption & AML

The principal instruments are the Law on Preventing and Combating Corruption, the Law on the Fight against Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, the Public Procurement Code and the corruption provisions of the Penal Code. A 2021 law transferred the functions of the former anti-corruption special court and anti-corruption police brigade to the Prosecutor General's office, the courts of appeal and the judicial police. Other bodies include the Financial Intelligence Unit established in 2008, the Court of Auditors, the General Inspectorate of the State and the Ombudsman.

General information compiled 2026-11-04 from the sources listed below. It is not legal advice; TDSC works with qualified local counsel on questions of law.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters Touching Burundi

TDSC scopes Burundi engagements from Nashville, beginning with a review of what the client needs to know, what lawful sources can answer it and whether any work inside the country is necessary. Much can be done from outside: international sanctions and enforcement lists, partner-country trade and corporate records, published research and court records abroad. Where documents must be retrieved from the Commercial Court or other offices, TDSC coordinates qualified, appropriately authorised local professionals working with Burundian counsel, and confirms in advance what methods they will use. Personal data is minimised and transferred under the 2026 law's cross-border rules. TDSC does not claim access to government systems, does not use pretexting and does not provide legal advice.

TDSC has no office in Burundi. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope. TDSC does not provide legal advice.

Typical Matters

Where Investigative Work Involving Burundi Concentrates

01

Gold and 3T sourcing reviews

Desk research and coordinated local verification on exporters, comptoirs and intermediaries in gold, tin, tantalum and tungsten, where published research describes gaps between declared output and partner-country imports, supporting buyers and refiners applying due diligence and responsible-sourcing standards.

02

Coffee supply chain integrity

Background checks on washing stations, cooperatives, exporters and buyers in a sector that generates most of Burundi's export earnings, for roasters, traders and certifiers assessing ownership, licensing, payment practices and reputational exposure in their supply chain.

03

Aid partner and grantee vetting

Integrity due diligence on implementing partners, contractors and suppliers for development agencies, NGOs and foundations, focusing on ownership, political exposure, procurement history and any adverse reporting, conducted within the limits of the 2026 data protection law.

04

Cross-border trade counterparties

Verification of importers, transporters and distributors operating along East African Community corridors through Tanzania, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where documentation gaps, customs exemptions and foreign exchange access raise integrity questions.

05

Land and asset research

Coordinated retrieval of land, registry and court documents by qualified local professionals to support title verification, enforcement planning or dispute strategy, recognising that land allocation and titling are documented areas of irregularity and that records are often paper-based.

Questions

Burundi: Frequently Asked Questions

Can a Burundian company's shareholders be checked online?

Not reliably. We have not identified a public online search of the Registre du Commerce et du Crédit Mobilier, and there is no beneficial ownership register. Extracts are generally obtained in person at the Commercial Court in Bujumbura through a local agent. TDSC combines such extracts, where lawfully obtainable, with records of foreign parent companies and trade partners to build a fuller picture.

Does Burundi now have a data protection law?

Yes. Law No. 1/03 of 10 March 2026 on the Protection of Personal Data sets lawful bases for processing, special rules for sensitive data and conditions for transfers abroad. The Personal Data Protection Agency it creates was reported in April 2026 as not yet operational, so implementing decrees and guidance are still expected and the practical position may change.

Are private investigators licensed in Burundi?

We have not identified a specific licensing regime for private investigators. That uncertainty is a reason for caution rather than a gap to exploit. TDSC scopes any local enquiry with Burundian counsel, limits it to lawful methods such as document retrieval and consented interviews, and uses qualified local professionals rather than sending its own staff into the field.

How do you approach gold sourcing questions involving Burundi?

We start with documentary evidence available outside the country, including export and import statistics, refinery and buyer disclosures, corporate records of trading houses and published investigative research. Where local confirmation of a licence or exporter identity is needed, it is obtained through qualified local professionals. Findings are framed to support the client's own responsible-sourcing obligations, not to certify origin.

Which language will source documents be in?

Most official and court documents are in French, with Kirundi used in administration and some proceedings. Laws are cited by number and date. TDSC reviews French-language material directly and arranges certified translation where a document will be relied on in proceedings or regulatory filings outside Burundi.
